design_rationale: Explicit randomized controlled trial: "A random assignment stratified by age... Random numbers generated by computer were employed," with a research assistant generating the sequence and allocating participants.

domain_judgments.rationale: Computer-generated stratified random sequence created and allocated by an independent research assistant with no participant contact, and baseline characteristics were balanced apart from one chance difference (psychiatric comorbidity, P=0.02).
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The research assistant, who had no contact with the participants, generated the random assignment sequence, and assigned the participants (recruited by the researchers) to one or other group. This method ensured blinding up to the point when interventions were assigned."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants and intervention-delivering researchers were unblinded (unavoidable for an informed-consent intervention), contamination between socially connected women was acknowledged by the authors, and the analysis excluded non-contactable participants rather than being strictly intention-to-treat.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "The participants and the researchers administering the intervention had knowledge of the group to which each participant had been assigned... The transfer of the experimental information provided to participants early in the study to other women called for screening at later dates is another possible source of bias"

domain_judgments.rationale: 79 of 434 randomized women (~18%) were lost, mainly to failed telephone follow-up, with balanced attrition between arms but no sensitivity analysis; additionally the cancer-worry outcome was available for only ~28% of participants because the scale was added after study start.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Numbers of women assigned to the standard information (control) and experimental information (intervention) groups were 216 and 218, respectively. Of these totals, 178 of the control and 177 of the IG were included in the analyses... The analysis of worries about cancer was performed with only 62 control and 59 IG participants, because this scale was introduced in the study some time after it had been initiated."

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcomes used validated/previously described instruments applied identically to both arms, but the knowledge questionnaire was tailored to the content of the Cochrane leaflet given only to the intervention arm, outcomes were self-reported by unblinded participants, and the follow-up telephone interviews appear to have been conducted by the same non-blinded researchers (only the statistician/research assistant were blinded).
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "the knowledge analysis questionnaire... was further modified to take into account BCS benefits and risks as described in a 2008 document... developed by the Nordic Cochrane Centre"

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered (NCT01335906) with a protocol supplied and a pre-specified primary outcome, but registration occurred after recruitment began, knowledge was reported both dichotomously and continuously, and additional unplanned subgroup/multivariable analyses were presented.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Participants were recruited between January 2011 and September 2012. The study was registered (ClinicalTrials. gov Identifier: NCT01335906) in April 2011."

overall_summary: Allocation was securely randomized with balanced baseline groups, but the unavoidable lack of participant/interviewer blinding, ~18% attrition (and much greater missingness for the cancer-worry outcome), a knowledge questionnaire aligned to the intervention material, and registration occurring after recruitment began raise some concerns. No single domain reached high risk, so the overall judgment is "some concerns".

design_rationale: Women aged 48–49 were selected and allocated to receive the new or old leaflet by a computer-assisted random procedure: "The 24 participants from each practice were selected by a computer-assisted random procedure, and the group allotment process was also random," with a published protocol and trial registration (DRKS00004271).

domain_judgments.rationale: Computer-assisted random allocation stratified within practices with pseudonymized mailing concealing allocation from participants and practices; baseline characteristics were comparable except a chance difference in marital status, which was adjusted for in models.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The 24 participants from each practice were selected by a computer-assisted random procedure, and the group allotment process was also random. ... The participants and their family physicians were blinded with respect to group allotment

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants were blinded to which leaflet version they received, but adherence to the instruction to read the leaflet before answering was unverifiable and the authors note women "filled out the questionnaires at home, and thus may have consulted external references"; analysis was restricted to responders rather than all randomized women.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The participants were asked by letter to fill out the questionnaire after reading the leaflet and to send it back in an envelope that was also enclosed in the mailing.

domain_judgments.rationale: Over half of randomized women (53%) provided no outcome data, and because non-responders' characteristics and screening attitudes are unknown (authors concede results "may be biased in the positive direction"), results could plausibly be biased by missingness despite balanced numbers returned per arm.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: 185 questionnaires were filled out and returned by each of the two groups (response rate, 46.7%)

domain_judgments.rationale: The outcome was identically self-reported in both arms by blinded participants, but the single yes/no hypothetical intention item is a surrogate for actual screening uptake and the questionnaire was only partly validated, introducing measurement concerns.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: their willingness to undergo screening was only asked about theoretically, and not verified by actual participation

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was registered with a published protocol and the pre-specified primary endpoint and analysis (likelihood-ratio chi-square, two-tailed) were reported as planned; subgroup/interaction findings are transparently labelled post-hoc and exploratory.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: The statistical analysis was predetermined only with respect to the primary analysis and the establishment of secondary endpoints. No correction for multiplicity was made in the model search

overall_summary: Allocation was properly computer-randomized and concealed, with a registered protocol and pre-specified primary analysis, but only 46.7% of mailed questionnaires were returned, leaving outcome data missing for more than half of randomized women whose attitudes may differ systematically. This substantial attrition, together with reliance on a hypothetical self-reported intention outcome and unverifiable leaflet reading, drives an overall high risk of bias.

design_rationale: Participants who consented were explicitly allocated to intervention or control using computer-generated random numbers: "Women who provided consent and their e-mail address were randomised to the intervention condition (leaflet) or the control condition (no leaflet) by computer-generated random numbers."

domain_judgments.rationale: A credible computer-generated random sequence was used and baseline characteristics were similar across arms, but allocation concealment is not described and the resulting group sizes were notably unequal (703 vs 609; 54% vs 46%) without explanation of an unequal allocation ratio.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Women who provided consent and their e-mail address were randomised to the intervention condition (leaflet) or the control condition (no leaflet) by computer-generated random numbers." ... "The 1312 included participants were randomised to the leaflet (n = 703, 54 %) and the control condition (n = 609, 46 %)."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew whether they received the leaflet (no blinding possible), actual reading of/adherence to the leaflet was not verified, and analyses were restricted to questionnaire completers rather than following an intention-to-treat principle on all 1312 randomized women; the authors themselves note the study context likely intensified leaflet reading relative to practice.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "We expected that in the context of the study, participants were more likely to read the leaflet more intensively than when they received it with the screening appointment invitation. Therefore, the found effects on knowledge and explicit attitudes may be smaller in practice."

domain_judgments.rationale: Only 988/1312 randomized women (75%) provided follow-up questionnaire data, attendance data were available for 904, and crucially the priming-task (implicit association) outcome was available for only ~48–53% of participants with statistically significant differential completion between arms (57% leaflet vs 49% control, p<0.01) and demonstrable differences between completers and non-completers, which the authors acknowledge could have caused selection bias.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A weakness of this study was that only about half of the participants completed the priming task. This reduced the power of the analyses and could have led to selection bias. Comparing demographics, the participants who completed the priming task were more often higher educated, less often retired, and more often first-time invitees than the participants who did not complete the priming task."

domain_judgments.rationale: Attendance was objectively obtained from the screening registry and knowledge/attitude instruments were previously used validated measures applied identically in both arms, but the primary knowledge and explicit-attitude outcomes were self-reported by unblinded participants (with acknowledged social-desirability pressure), and the web-based priming task was administered in uncontrolled home settings with post hoc exclusion of one ambiguous target word.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Possibly participants may have felt a pressure to give socially desired answers, which made the topic partly socially sensitive" ... "Due to misconceptions regarding one of the targets (double meaning in Dutch) the response times for this target were excluded for analyses."

domain_judgments.rationale: No trial registration or pre-specified analysis plan is cited, the primary outcome is ambiguous (sample size was powered on response time, yet knowledge/attitudes are emphasised), and multiple outcome operationalizations (continuous knowledge score vs. 'sufficient knowledge' cut-off, intention vs. attendance, three primes), subgroup analyses of first-time invitees, and post hoc ANCOVA covariate selection create scope for selective reporting.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Sample size calculation indicated that 834 women needed to participate to be able to show an effect in response time with 80 % power" ... "Subsequently, a repeated measures ANCOVA was performed taking into account the covariates that were significant in the correlations analyses."

overall_summary: Overall risk of bias is high, driven by missing outcome data (D3): only 75% of randomized women contributed follow-up data and the implicit-association outcome was available for roughly half of participants with significantly differential completion between arms (57% vs 49%) and documented differences between completers and non-completers. Remaining domains raise some concerns (unconcealed allocation with unequal arm sizes, unavoidable lack of participant blinding with non-ITT completer-only analysis, self-reported outcomes subject to social desirability, and no pre-registration with ambiguous primary outcome and multiple analytic choices).

design_rationale: Explicit two-stage parallel 1:1 cluster RCT: 40 Basic Health Areas were "selected and randomised to intervention or control using computer-generated blocks of size two", with random sampling of women within clusters; trial registered (NCT03046004) and reported per CONSORT.

domain_judgments.rationale: Allocation sequence was computer-generated and concealed from interviewers, but baseline imbalances were present (attitudes towards knowing benefits/harms p=0.029/0.011, overall attitude score difference 0.39 (0.15,0.64), previous mammogram use 83.7% vs 75.6%, p=0.052), which in a cluster-randomised design with differential recruitment/response (260 vs 264 baseline from 954 vs 1117 selected) raises some concern, though authors adjusted in mixed models.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Basic Health Areas (BHAs) were stratified by socioeconomic level and 40 of them were selected and randomised to intervention or control using computer-generated blocks of size two... The random allocation sequence was generated by a statistician with no contact with the participants (MR)."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants necessarily knew the content of the leaflet they received (unavoidable in an information intervention) and 3% did not read the leaflet through; analysis was complete-case among those completing both questionnaires rather than strict intention-to-treat on all randomised women, though delivery of materials was standardised and interviewers were blinded.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Interviewers invited the selected women using the phrase 'a study about information on advantages and disadvantages of breast screening' without mentioning specific terms as false positive or overdiagnosis... trained interviewers, not aware of the women's allocation, contacted them by phone"

domain_judgments.rationale: Of 2071 randomly selected women only 524 completed baseline and 400 completed the post-intervention questionnaire (≈24% of selected; 37.6% of invited and eligible), with attrition from baseline to follow-up of ~24% and no imputation, so substantial and potentially differential missingness (attitudes already differed at baseline) could bias the effect estimates despite a limited sensitivity analysis.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "only 56% of women in the initially selected sample could be reached and only around 38% of those invited completed the study... Missing values imputation was not done in women lost to follow-up or who had not completed the post-intervention questionnaire."

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcomes were self-reported via identical validated-scale questionnaires in both arms (participation verified from program records), but informed choice is a composite requiring arbitrary thresholds, items were modified from the original and translated without formal cross-cultural validation, and participants were unblinded self-reporters.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "we did not use open numerical questions (asking for absolute frequencies of the outcomes), but instead, we used multiple choice questions on frequency categories... we did not perform a cross-cultural adaptation/validation"

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered with a published protocol defining the primary outcome (informed choice) and secondary outcomes, analyses followed the pre-specified plan, and results are reported comprehensively with a CONSORT checklist.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "We performed the statistical analysis as planned in the protocol [14]... The InforMa study was registered with the ClinicalTrials.gov registry, number NCT03046004."

overall_summary: Well-registered, protocol-driven cluster RCT with concealed computer-generated allocation and pre-specified analyses, but only ~38% of invited eligible women completed the study with no imputation for missing outcome data, giving high risk in D3; baseline attitude imbalances, unblinded participants, and composite self-reported, non-cross-culturally-validated outcomes add further concerns, so the overall judgment is high risk of bias.

design_rationale: The paper explicitly describes a community-based, parallel-group RCT with computer-generated random allocation sequence and 1:1 allocation using permuted blocks: "A programmer who had no contact with participants generated the randomisation sequence using a computer system that was inaccessible until after recruitment"; trial registered (ACTRN12613001035718).

domain_judgments.rationale: Computer-generated sequence with permuted blocks, concealed from recruiters/interviewers until after enrolment, and Table 1 shows closely similar baseline demographics, knowledge, attitudes and intentions consistent with chance.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "A programmer who had no contact with participants generated the randomisation sequence using a computer system that was inaccessible until after recruitment; therefore, interviewers were unaware of the materials that women would receive (ensuring allocation concealment). We assigned participants to either the intervention or control group in a 1:1 ratio with permuted block sizes of four and eight."

domain_judgments.rationale: Participants were masked as to which booklet was the intervention, interviewers were masked until the final question, adherence was high and balanced (97% vs 98% read the whole booklet; similar rates of external information seeking), and an as-randomised (modified ITT) analysis with imputation sensitivity analyses was used.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "Women knew they would receive one of two versions of an information booklet but did not know how these dif ered or which one was the intervention... we included in our primary analysis all participants as randomised, except for those lost to follow-up and those for whom some outcome data were missing"

domain_judgments.rationale: Attrition was low (~7%) and nearly identical across arms, and two prespecified multiple-imputation sensitivity analyses gave unchanged results, making bias from missingness unlikely.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "21 women in the intervention group and 20 controls were lost to follow-up; a further ten women assigned to the intervention and 11 controls did not answer all questions on attitudes... Results for informed choice and its components did not change when missing values were imputed... Sociodemographic characteristics were similar for women who did and did not provide follow-up data."

domain_judgments.rationale: Outcome measures were standardised, validated where available, scored with an a priori marking scheme, and interviewers/analysts were largely masked; however, the primary outcome is participant-reported and depends on an investigator-chosen composite threshold, the knowledge items map closely onto the intervention content (content-congruent measurement favouring the intervention arm), and some overdetection items had to be worded differently for controls.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "We designed the follow-up interview to ensure the group assignment was unclear to the interviewer until the fi nal question... The control decision aid did not mention overdetection, therefore, these questions used the phrase 'be(ing) diagnosed and treated for a breast cancer that is not harmful' to refer to overdetection."

domain_judgments.rationale: The trial was prospectively registered with a published protocol, the primary outcome, knowledge thresholds and analysis set were prespecified, and the alternative conceptual-knowledge-only definition is transparently labelled a sensitivity analysis rather than substituted for the primary result.
domain_judgments.evidence_quote: "This trial is registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, number ACTRN12613001035718... We scored answers with a marking scheme that we developed a priori... We set a threshold a priori to defi ne adequate knowledge for informed choice... In accordance with our published protocol, we included in our primary analysis all participants as randomised"

overall_summary: This was a well-conducted, prospectively registered RCT with concealed computer randomisation, balanced baseline characteristics, masked participants/interviewers/analysts, very low and balanced attrition with confirmatory imputation analyses, and prespecified outcomes and thresholds. The overall judgment of "some concerns" is driven solely by outcome measurement (D4): the primary outcome is a self-reported composite whose knowledge component is closely congruent with the intervention booklet's content and whose overdetection items had to be reworded for the control arm, which could inflate the apparent effect.
